L0@P0: S E C R E T
L1@P0: H.M.S. LEDBURY
L2@P0: OPERATION PEDESTAL — LETTER OF PROCEEDINGS.
L3@P0: Sunday 9th August 1942
L4@P0: 0300 Sailed from Gibraltar
L5@P0: 1400 Sighted convoy.
L6@P0: 1440 Took up station on screen of convoy.
L7@P0: Monday 10th August l942
L8@P0: 2300 Left convoy and proceeded to oiler.
L9@P0: Tuesday 11th August 1942
L10@P0: Oiled from 0700 to 0819 from DINGLEDALE, taking 101 tons.
L11@P0: 0950 In station as starboard wing ship of screen.
L12@P0: 1314 H.M.S. EAGLE was hit by torpedo/s.
L13@P0: 1318 DERWENT ordered me to stand by EAGLE.
L14@P0: 1225 EAGLE sank. There were many survivors in the oil patches in the
L15@P0: water and one destroyer and the tug JAUNTY were stopped
L16@P0: picking them up. As we reached survivors, we were ordered by
L17@P0: D.19 to rejoin convoy.
L18@P0: 1420 High level bombing attack.
L19@P0: 2058 Shallow dive-bombing by Junkers 88s started. One plane was
L20@P0: seen to be on fire. The port Oerlikon hit one plane. (Many other
L21@P0: ships were firing at this machine).
L22@P0: 2010 Ordered to A/A station. 1 cable on the starboard beam of No. 43.
L23@P0: Wednesday 12th August 1942
L24@P0: 0627 Ordered by NELSON to investigate periscope reported on
L25@P0: starboard quarter of No. 43.
L26@P0: 0710 NELSON reported submarine periscope bearing north of her.
L27@P0-1: page 1Single scare charges were dropped to cover INDOMITABLE from
L28@P1: this submarine, and destroyers astern appeared to follow up
L29@P1: this contact.
L30@P1: 0900 An air attack by Junkers 88s developed on the convoy.
L31@P1: 0915 One Junkers 88 crashed bearing 058 degrees. Four small bombs
L32@P1: were seen to go by the bridge, landing on the starboard aide,
L33@P1: and a large bomb near missed the port quarter.
L34@P1: 0930 Ordered to fill in gaps in the screen caused by ships falling back
L35@P1: on contact. On the way to this position three airmen were
L36@P1: seen coming down by parachute. One was picked up and
L37@P1: found to be German, so the other two were left. He stated that
L38@P1: the last raid consisted of German airmen flying Junkers 88s from
L39@P1: Sicily; and that he had been shot down by close range weapons
L40@P1: from the convoy. The most interesting thing about him was that
L41@P1: the nails of his boots were made of wood.
L42@P1: 1215 An attack by dive-bombers. Two groups approached from
L43@P1: ahead, but neither got over the convoy. Two were shot down
L44@P1: by gunfire.
L45@P1: 1238 Resumed station on the starboard side of the convoy
L46@P1: 1240 Torpedo bombing attack took place from the port side and
L47@P1: fourteen torpedo bombers were sighted on the starboard side.
L48@P1: These were driven off by gunfire, one being shot down. There
L49@P1: was no damage to the convoy.
L50@P1: 1318 An attack by Junkers 88s started whilst our own fighters were
L51@P1: landed for refuelling. One near miss off our port quarter.
L52@P1: One ship in the convoy was damaged. H.M.S. BRAMHAM
L53@P1: stood by her.
L54@P1: 1700 A submarine was forced to the surface astern and sunk by a
L55@P1: Tribal class destroyer.
L56@P1: 1857 Junkers 67s dropped parachute mines which all fell clear.
L57@P1: 1859 12 torpedo bombers approached from the starboard side but
L58@P1: were turned away by gunfire.
L59@P1: At the same time, Junkers 87s carried out dive-bombing
L60@P1: attacks, and H.M.S. INDOMITABLE was hit.
L61@P1: 1900 Force “Z” retired
L62@P1: 1950 The convoy was in process of forming two lines with the three
L63@P1: T.S.D.S. destroyers ahead, and the remaining ships in their A/A
L64@P1: stations in the column of the convoy.
L65@P1-2: page 2A signal, “Form two columns” was still flying, but most
L66@P2: ships were anticipating the movement and moving to their new
L67@P2: positions.
L68@P2: 1956 H.M. Ships NIGERIA and CAIRO and the tanker Ohio were
L69@P2: torpedoed.
L70@P2: The convoy carried out an emergency turn to starboard,
L71@P2: and most destroyers turned back to stand by the damaged
L72@P2: cruisers.
L73@P2: 2000 We were in station on the starboard side of the convoy ⎼ about
L74@P2: half way up ⎼ which was now roughly in two columns with
L75@P2: MANCHESTER, KENYA and PATHFINDER ahead.
L76@P2: A cruiser reported aircraft detected by R/D/F on the port
L77@P2: bow of the convoy and ship was taken through the convoy to get
L78@P2: to the engaged side; but a heavy and sustained attack by Junkers
L79@P2: 88s dive-bombing developed when we were in between the
L80@P2: columns.
L81@P2: Things were very warm for a few minutes, two ships were
L82@P2: hit, one blowing up and making a huge mass of burning petrol
L83@P2: on the water, the other remaining afloat but on fire.
L84@P2: Torpedo planes were now sighted on the starboard bow
L85@P2: very close.
L86@P2: The light was failing quickly.
L87@P2: We engaged the torpedo planes, but one delivered a very
L88@P2: good attack, dropping two torpedoes. Another ship blew up, and
L89@P2: I think the BRISBANE STAR was torpedoed at this time.
L90@P2: Told MANCHESTER we were standing by the damaged
L91@P2: ships, but in the darkness sighted six ships steaming on various
L92@P2: courses, mostly in a north or north-westerly direction.
L93@P2: I called up the nearest ship and ordered course 1200 which
L94@P2: I think she was turning round to. This ship was the
L95@P2: MELBOURNE STAR. The other ships were follows and hailed by
L96@P2: Ardente; told to turn to 1200 ; to make their best speed that the
L97@P2: Admiral and naval escort were proceeding slowly down the
L98@P2: coast waiting for them. The ALMERIA LYKES was furthest to the
L99@P2: westward and was the only one of the ships who queried this
L100@P2: order.
L101@P2: I then returned to the OHIO intending to take her in tow,
L102@P2: but she reported that she could steam with her steering aft but
L103@P2-3: page 3had no compass. We switched on a brighter stern light and told
L104@P3: her to follow us to Malta.
L105@P3: I realised now that if the stragglers continued on 1200 they
L106@P3: would pass to the east of Zembra and the minefield. I made an
L107@P3: emergency signal informing C.S.10 that stragglers had been
L108@P3: ordered to steer 1200.
L109@P3: I also informed HMS PENN with whom I was in V/S touch
L110@P3: at this time, that the survivors from the damaged ships had not
L111@P3: been picked up and I was going on with the oiler.
L112@P3: It seemed a very long time before we got clear of the glare
L113@P3: of the burning ships. The oiler was grand. She yawed heavily at
L114@P3: the beginning, but was soon steadied and we had worked up to
L115@P3: 15.5 knots before reaching Cape Bon.
L116@P3: During the night, four spectacular E Boat battles were
L117@P3: sighted just ahead around the next corner (At 0204, 0332, 0345
L118@P3: and 0431).
L119@P3: Thursday 13th August 1942
L120@P3: 0304 Three merchant ships were sighted whilst rounding
L121@P3: Kelibia. I think one of these was the BRISBANE STAR.
L122@P3: ALMERIA LYKES was told to follow.
L123@P3: 0250 Sighted small patrol boat apparently towing a target
L124@P3: inshore off Kelibia. Fire was withheld as our policy was evasion.
L125@P3: During the morning three abandoned merchant ships
L126@P3: were passed, some of them with boats with flares close by. (One
L127@P3: passed at 0330 and two at 0431).
L128@P3: I did not feel very happy leaving these crews, but knew
L129@P3: PENN was astern of me and I would not risk stopping or losing
L130@P3: sight of the tanker.
L131@P3: 0514 A glow was sighted from which no R.D.F echo could be
L132@P3: obtained. The glow suddenly blew up leaving a small petrol fire
L133@P3: which only lasted about ten minutes. This was thought to be a
L134@P3: damaged E boat blowing up.
L135@P3: 0540 Convoy sighted
L136@P3: 0350 Led the tanker in astern of the line.
L137@P3-4: page 4I informed C.S.10 in ASHANTI that there were three
L138@P4: stopped merchant ships between there and position “R” and
L139@P4: three more under weigh astern of that.
L140@P4: 0730 I also informed him of the tanker's condition. Torpedo
L141@P4: planes flew in to distract attention from Junkers 88s which were
L142@P4: coming in from a height. We had detected these by R.D.F. but
L143@P4: could not sight them and were slow in opening fire on them.
L144@P4: The WAIMARAMA was hit, probably by about three or four
L145@P4: bombs, and blew up with a tremendous explosion leaving a
L146@P4: great pylon of flame on the sea. ASHANTI signalled me to pick
L147@P4: up survivors. I went to the scene, but did not think it possible
L148@P4: that anyone could survive such a terrific explosion or mass of
L149@P4: flames, but on approaching, men were seen in the water.
L150@P4: I cannot speak too highly of the sheer guts of these men.
L151@P4: They were singing and encouraging each other, and as I went
L152@P4: through them explaining by Ardente that I must get the ones
L153@P4: nearest the flames first, I received answers of “That's alright, sir.
L154@P4: Go and get the other chaps”.
L155@P4: The flames were spreading outward all the time ⎼ even to
L156@P4: windward ⎼ and at one time spread the whole length of the ship
L157@P4: while picking up two men close to the after nets. I had to go
L158@P4: astern, and these men were supported by my rescuers who
L159@P4: themselves were clinging onto the nets.
L160@P4: I twice had to pass a merchant seaman who was some way
L161@P4: away from the fire, and each time we passed he said, “Don't
L162@P4: forget the diver, sir”.
L163@P4: The last man to be picked up was on a raft which was
L164@P4: anchored to some sunken debris in the middle of the fire. Owing
L165@P4: to fatigue an order was, repeated wrongly, and I had to go
L166@P4: around again to get this man. I am deeply conscious that owing
L167@P4: to this mistake I increased his suffering and serious burns.
L168@P4: 45 survivors were picked up, one of whom was dead. He
L169@P4: was buried that evening with military honours.
L170@P4: Some time later it was discovered that we had survivors
L171@P4: from the WAIMARAMA and the MELBOURNE STAR onboard.
L172@P4: When the WAIMARAMA blew up, it happened so suddenly
L173@P4: that the MELBOURNE STAR steamed right through the flames.
L174@P4: Those aft ⎼ quite understandably ⎼ thought that their own ship
L175@P4-5: page 5had gone up and jumped over the side. It was a fine thing to find
L176@P5: this ship in harbour at Malta when we arrived.
L177@P5: My cause for anxiety during this retrieving of survivors
L178@P5: was the parachute mines which we had seen fall all around the
L179@P5: burning ship, but no mines or parachutes were sighted in the
L180@P5: water.
L181@P5: The ship was attacked by Junkers 88s during this period
L182@P5: but the attack was not pressed home after we opened fire. The
L183@P5: director claimed one plane shot down, but I did not see it.
L184@P5: 0934 Completed picking up survivors. By this time I estimated
L185@P5: that we were about 30 miles astern of the convoy and would
L186@P5: have to go very fast to catch them up before we turned around
L187@P5: and went home.
L188@P5: I knew that my fuel was the limiting factor for the speed
L189@P5: home of Force “X”.
L190@P5: A signal was made to C.S.10, “30 miles astern of convoy ⎼
L191@P5: interrogative rejoin or go home?”. Course was set to rejoin the
L192@P5: convoy.
L193@P5: 1050 An attack was made on LEDBURY by Junkers 88s. Near
L194@P5: misses as usual.
L195@P5: 1115 Found OHIO and DORSET with BRAMHAM standing by
L196@P5: DORSET and PENN dropping depth charges.
L197@P5: The convoy was about ten miles away being attacked from
L198@P5: the air.
L199@P5: C.S.10’s reply to my signal was received very corrupt,
L200@P5: apparently ordering me to go home, but I considered it had been
L201@P5: made before OHIO was stopped.
L202@P5: I suggested to PENN that I should take OHIO in tow was
L203@P5: coming up to do this, when I received a signal from V.A.M to
L204@P5: C.S.10 (R) LEDBURY suggesting that I should stand by
L205@P5: MANCHESTER in the Gulf of Hammamet.
L206@P5: A signal originated from S.O. Cruiser Force, had previously
L207@P5: been received, saying “Engine room flooded. Afire”.
L208@P5: In view of the delay in signals, and as PENN and
L209@P5: BRAMHAM were standing by these two ships, I proceeded at 24
L210@P5: knots to look for MANCHESTER in the Gulf of Hammamet.
L211@P5: 1345 Passed wreckage of WAIMARAMA.
L212@P5-6: page 61545 Two three-engined Italian bombers approached on the
L213@P6: port beam. 4" cease fire bells were rung in order not to
L214@P6: discourage them, and short bursts from Oerlikon and pom-pom
L215@P6: shot them both down in flames. The second one had time to
L216@P6: drop his torpedo whilst we were dealing with the first. This was
L217@P6: small, slow and a “W” type.
L218@P6: This success came at a very apt time as the ship’s company
L219@P6: were showing signs of very great fatigue, and the survivors
L220@P6: were, most understandably, jumpy. The whole ship was cheering
L221@P6: hard, and everything after this went with a swing.
L222@P6: 1630 Landfall was made.
L223@P6: 1700 Identified as Ras-Mahmur.
L224@P6: Course was set to follow the coast line looking for the
L225@P6: MANCHESTER. When we were almost certain that she was not
L226@P6: in the bay, the coast was closed, in case there might be any
L227@P6: survivors on the beach.
L228@P6: The signal station at NEBOEL started calling up “VHM -
L229@P6: VHA”. We did not reply.
L230@P6: The signal station at Hammamet made a flag signal, “Show
L231@P6: your signal letters”. We hoisted an Italian group consisting of
L232@P6: flag “I” and three other flags tied in knots so as to be unreadable.
L233@P6: This apparently satisfied the shore station as they hoisted a
L234@P6: large French ensign.
L235@P6: During this period I was showing no ensign. Unfortunately
L236@P6: we do not carry an Italian ensign.
L237@P6: I went on down the coast until 12 miles south of
L238@P6: Hammamet.
L239@P6: During this time there were enemy reports of a cruiser
L240@P6: near Zembra and two destroyers making for Pantellaria. I felt
L241@P6: very lonely, particularly as a signal from C.S.10 was
L242@P6: intercepted saying that LEDBURY was standing by OHIO.
L243@P6: 1900 Course was set to pass 5 miles south of Linosa. We altered
L244@P6: course after dark to rejoin OHIO.
L245@P6: I could not get a D/F bearing from PENN or BRAMHAM but
L246@P6: sighted their gunfire at first light the next day.
L247@P6: Friday 14th August 1942
L248@P6-7: page 7OHIO was stopped with no hope of getting her engines
L249@P7: going as she had been hit again whilst in tow of PENN.
L250@P7: A 6" manilla was passed from the tanker’s stern to my
L251@P7: midship oiling bollard, my idea being to take the stern to port,
L252@P7: whilst the minesweeper RYE towed her; but I put on too much
L253@P7: weight and RYE’s tow parted, PENN then ordered me to take the
L254@P7: tanker in tow from ahead, which I did, using the tanker’s tow
L255@P7: and a shackle of my cable. RYE took me in tow to keep the ship
L256@P7: from falling off, whilst PENN went alongside the starboard side
L257@P7: of the tanker to act as a drag to keep her straight.
L258@P7: My gunner, who was in charge of the towing party onboard
L259@P7: the tanker tried out all the tanker’s guns, which was as
L260@P7: well since at 1044 we were attacked by nine Stukas (Junkers
L261@P7: 87s).
L262@P7: We received a near miss within a few feet of the foc’sle,
L263@P7: which fortunately was an oil bomb and caused no casualties.
L264@P7: There was also a near miss astern.
L265@P7: The following is an extract from the ship's narrative: -
L266@P7: “Mr. Musham, Gunner of H.M.S. LEDBURY whilst acting
L267@P7: master of the OHIO (unpaid) fired six magazines of
L268@P7: Oerlikon ammunition at the dive bombers, and claimed
L269@P7: that he shot down one of them. The gun’s crews of PENN
L270@P7: confirmed this. He complained that he was forced to use
L271@P7: hosepipe firing instead of eyeshooting, as the sights had
L272@P7: already been stolen by the gunner of H.M.S. “LEDBURY”.
L273@P7: This was the last attack, and PENN and BRAMHAM
L274@P7: secured either side of the tanker, by magnificent seamanship
L275@P7: and endurance brought OHIO into Valletta Harbour.
L276@P7: Saturday 15th August 1942
L277@P7: 0315 Took oiler in tow in order to get her straight for the
L278@P7: channel.
L279@P7: With the help of an M.L. pushing my bows. I managed to
L280@P7: turn her 1400 in three hauls, turning her about 450 each time.
L281@P7: No damage or casualties were sustained in the ship. The
L282@P7: behaviour of the ship’s company throughout the operation was
L283@P7: exemplary, and no Commanding Officer could have wished for a
L284@P7: finer ship’s company.
L285@P7-8: page 8(Signed) Roger Hill
L286@P8: LIEUTENANT COMMANDER
L287@P8:  COMMANDING OFFICER – H.M.S. LEDBURY

L289@P8: Glossary
L290@P8: Ardente — A make of loudhailer manufactured by Ardente Acoustic Laboratories in
L291@P8: Guildford. [IWM]
L292@P8-9: page 9Oerlikon — A Swiss-designed autocannon originally used in aircraft. British-made
L293@P9: Oerlikon 20 mm cannons were delivered to the Royal Navy in March or April, 1941.
L294@P9: Pom-pom — A 2-pounder gun, officially the QF 2-pounder and universally known as
L295@P9: the pom-pom, was a 40 mm British autocannon, used as an anti-aircraft gun by the
L296@P9: Royal Navy.
